rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The month’s obligation entails honoring it through fasting for everyone who reaches it, whether resident or traveling; a resident’s ruling is to fast.
rows.anchor: من وجوب التعظيم المستفاد مما في أثره على كل من أدركه ومدركه إما حاضر أو مسافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Witnessing the month means reaching or experiencing it; it is not well paraphrased as merely knowing that the crescent appeared.
rows.anchor: ولا يحسن أن يقال من علم الهلال فليصم

words: وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍۢ
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One objection says the detailed coordinating conjunction makes the sick and traveling a category distinct from those who witnessed the month.
rows.anchor: والعاطف التفصيلي يقتضي المغايرة بينهما كذا قيل

words: وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍۢ
rows.speaker: أكثر النحويين
rows.claim: Mention of the sick supports treating them as a specification of those who witnessed; most grammarians parse “the month” as object, making the fa causal or sequential rather than explanatory.
rows.anchor: أكثر النحويين إلى أن الشهر مفعول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s ease-giving and rejection of hardship express His abundant mercy and compassion in making this exception.
rows.anchor: لغاية رأفته وسعة رحمته

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites infer that a person can do what God does not will: a sick or traveling person who fasts to exhaustion acts against the ease God wills.
rows.anchor: وأستدل المعتزلة بالآية على أنه قد يقع من العبد ما لا يريده الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuttal is that God wills ease by permitting the sick and traveler to break the fast; the permission is fulfilled by the command to make up the days.
rows.anchor: ورد بأن الله تعالى أراد التيسير وعدم التعسير في حقهما بإباحة الفطر وقد حصل بمجرد الأمر

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr interprets divine willing here as demanding; al-Alusi says this entails the Muʿtazilite view that God’s will concerning human acts is command.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر تفسير الإرادة هنا بالطلب وفيه إلتزام لمذهب الإعتزال

words: وَمَن كَانَ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām clauses can be attached to an implied “He legislated,” signaled by the fasting command: complete the month’s count by fasting it when present and making up excused missed days without loss.
rows.anchor: فعل محذوف دل عليه ( فمن شهد منكم الشهر ) إلخ أي وشرع لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Completing the count preserves the month’s blessings and rewards whether the month has fewer days or is complete.
rows.anchor: فتحصلوا خيراته ولا يفوتكم شيء من بركاته نقصت أيامه أو كملت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis treats each lām as the reason for its own implied act: God obligated make-up days, taught their method, and granted the exemption.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن تكون عللا لأفعال مقدرة كل فعل مع علة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links takbīr to the make-up ruling and gratitude to the concession; shifting to “perhaps” subtly presents gratitude as hoped-for despite strong grounds for it.
rows.anchor: علة الترخيص والتيسير وتغيير الأسلوب للإشارة إلى هذا المطلوب بمنزلة المرجو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clauses may instead depend on an implied “so it is easy for you” or “so you may know what to do”; some are rationale by way of making the preceding rulings clear.
rows.anchor: ليسهل أو لتعلموا علة لما سبق بإعتبار الإعلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further option attaches the lām clauses to “ease” after “God wills,” taking the lām as purposive and possibly extra after a verb of willing.
rows.anchor: واللام زائدة مقدرة بعدها أن وزيدت كما قيل : بعد فعل الإرادة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A reported analysis takes the lām as equivalent to “that,” but then gratitude must coordinate with “He wills,” producing an incoherent construction and disconnected clauses.
rows.anchor: إنها بمعنى أن كما في الرضى إلا أنه يلزم على هذا الوجه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some avoid the earlier parses by understanding an ellipsis: God granted the concession because He wills ease, while completing the count and gratitude explain the rulings.
rows.anchor: عدل بعضهم عن الجميع وجعل الكلام من الميل مع المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Takbīr” here figuratively means praise and glorification, of which declaring God greatest is one kind; the preposition “upon” fits this meaning.
rows.anchor: والمراد من التكبير الحمد والثناء مجازا لكونه فردا منه ولذلك عدى بعلي

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam reports that the takbīr is the glorification on the day of Eid.
rows.anchor: وأخرج إبن المنذر وغيره عن زيد بن أسلم أن المراد به التكبير يوم العيد

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to say that the takbīr is made on sighting the crescent of Shawwāl.
rows.anchor: أنه التكبير عند الإهلال

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Muslims should glorify God upon seeing Shawwāl’s crescent until Eid ends, citing the verse; al-Alusi notes this reading does not explain the prior rulings.
rows.anchor: حق على المسلمين إذا نظروا إلى هلال شوال أن يكبروا الله تعالى حتى يفرعوا من عيدهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle “mā” may be a verbal noun (“for His guiding you”) or a relative pronoun (“that to which He guided you”).
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن تكون مصدرية وأن تكون موصولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude includes more than verbal praise, making it an apt rationale for the practical gift of the concession.
rows.anchor: والمراد من الشكر ما هو أعم من الثناء ولذا ناسب أن يجعل طلبه تعليلا للترخيص

rows.speaker: أبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: Abū Bakr’s transmission from ʿĀṣim reads “litukammilū” with a doubled mīm.
rows.anchor: أبو بكر عن عاصم ( ولتكملوا ) بالتشديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once you have performed and finished the rites of pilgrimage, remember God as you used to remember your fathers after the pilgrimage, boasting of their deeds.
rows.anchor: أي أديتم عباداتكم الحجية وفرغتم منها فأذكروا الله كذكركم آباءكم

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that in pre-Islamic times people sat after pilgrimage all day recalling their fathers’ deeds and lineage; the verse redirected this remembrance to God.
rows.anchor: كان أهل الجاهلية يجلسون بعد الحج فيذكرون أيام آبائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing makes “stronger remembrance” genitive with “remembrance,” treating remembrance as an agent by metaphor: remember God as you remember your fathers or more intensely.
rows.anchor: مجرور معطوف على الذكر بجعل الذكر ذاكرا على المجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “stronger” coordinates with the genitive pronoun under the permissive Kūfan analysis, meaning remembrance of people whose remembrance exceeds yours.
rows.anchor: على ما أضيف إليه بناءا على مذهب الكوفيين المجوزين للعطف على الضمير المجرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An accusative parsing coordinates “stronger” with “your fathers,” taking “remembrance” passively: God is more remembered than your fathers.
rows.anchor: منصوب بالعطف على ( آباءكم ) و ( ذكرا ) من فعل المبني للمفعول

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An ellipsis may instead mean: let your remembrance of God be stronger than your remembrance of your fathers.
rows.anchor: أي ليكن ذكركم الله تعالى أشد من ذكركم آباءكم

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr prefers taking “stronger” as a circumstantial accusative modifying “remembrance”; delaying “remembrance” gives the verse its cadence and avoids awkward repetition.
rows.anchor: في البحر أن يكون ( أشد ) نصب على الحال من ذكرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The circumstantial parse is challenged: “or stronger” without “remembrance” would be expected, since the desired object is remembrance characterized as stronger, not remembering while in a stronger state.
rows.anchor: على هذا الوجه أن يقال أو أشد بدون ( ذكرا )

rows.speaker: الواحدى
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says ʿUmar, Muʿādh ibn Jabal, and a group of Anṣār asked the Prophet for a ruling because wine and gambling destroy reason and consume wealth; this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: نزلت في عمر بن الخطاب . ومعاذ بن جبل . ونفر من الإنصار

rows.speaker: بعض الروايات
rows.claim: Another account says the verse first came after the Prophet arrived in Medina; people continued drinking until ʿAbd al-Raḥmān’s feast, where intoxicated ʿAlī omitted “no” while leading prayer, prompting 4:43.
rows.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم قدم المدينة وهم يشربون الخمر ويأكلون الميسر

rows.speaker: بعض الروايات
rows.claim: At a later feast hosted by ʿUtban, Saʿd’s boasting poem insulted the Anṣār; a man struck and wounded him, after which Saʿd appealed to the Prophet and the final prohibition was revealed days after al-Aḥzāb; ʿUmar declared they had stopped.
rows.anchor: ثم اتخذ عتبان بن مالك صنيعا ودعا رجالا من المسلمين فيهم سعد بن أبي وقاص

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī says he would not pray from a minaret built over a well into which wine had fallen, nor let his animal graze where wine had fallen into the sea.
rows.anchor: وعن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه لو وقعت قطرة منها في بئر

rows.speaker: إبن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says that if he dipped his finger into wine, it would not follow him, an image of complete avoidance.
rows.anchor: وعن إبن عمر رضي الله تعالى عنهما لو أدخلت أصبعي فيها لم تتبعني

rows.speaker: الإمام أبي حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa defines wine narrowly as grape juice that boils, ferments, and casts up foam; the term is explained as covering the mind, like a woman’s veil covers her face.
rows.anchor: التي من ماء العنب إذا غلى وأشتد وقذف بالزبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed etymologies connect wine with covering, mixing with the mind, or being left until it matures; these accounts are close in sense, and the noun may be an agent, patient, or intensive verbal noun.
rows.anchor: لأنها تخالط العقل وخامره داء خالطه

rows.speaker: الإمامان
rows.claim: Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad do not require foam to appear; fermentation alone suffices because the intoxicating cause is then present.
rows.anchor: وذهب الإمامان إلى عدم اشتراط القذف ويكفي الإشتداد لأن المعنى المحرم يحصل به

rows.speaker: الإمام أبي حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa regards boiling as the beginning of fermentation and foam rising and settling as its completion; legal consequences attach to completion, as with the fixed penalty and sale prohibition.
rows.anchor: وللإمام أن الغليان بداية الشدة وكمالها بقذف الزبد وسكونه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some jurists adopt Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad’s threshold for the drinking ban as a precaution.
rows.anchor: وأخذ بعضهم بقولهما في حرمة الشرب إحتياطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Hanafi position and common Arabic usage, calling a drink from other substances “wine” is figurative; some people argue that the word is literal for every intoxicant.
rows.anchor: مجاز عندنا وهو المعروف عند أهل اللغة

rows.speaker: الشيخان وأبو داؤد والترمذي والنسائي
rows.claim: Reports in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and Sunan collections state that every intoxicant is wine.
rows.anchor: كل مسكرخمر

rows.speaker: أبو داؤد
rows.claim: Abū Dāwūd reports that the prohibition was revealed for wine made from five sources—grapes, dates, wheat, barley, and corn—and that wine is what clouds the mind.
rows.anchor: من العنب والتمر والحنطة والشعير والذرة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Muslim reports from Abū Hurayra that wine comes from these two trees, with the Prophet pointing to the vine and date-palm.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة ( الخمر ) من هاتين الشجرتين وأشار إلى الكرم والنخلة

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that grape wine was scarce when wine was prohibited and most of their wine came from unripe dates and dates.
rows.anchor: حرمت الخمر حين حرمت وما يتخذ من خمر الأعناب إلا قليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi reads these reports as teaching the legal rule that all intoxicants are forbidden, not defining Arabic vocabulary; the Prophet’s mission was guidance, while his audience already knew Arabic.
rows.anchor: ويمكن أن يجاب أن المقصود من ذلك كله بيان الحكم وتعليم أن ما أسكر حرام كالخمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deriving “wine” from its covering the mind does not prove that the word covers every intoxicant; “star” likewise derives from appearing but names a particular star.
rows.anchor: فإن النجم مشتق من الظهور ثم هو أسم خاص للنجم المعروف لا لكل ما ظهر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A middle position says Arabic uses “wine” literally for intoxicating grape juice and figuratively for other sources, while Islamic law made it a technical term for every intoxicant, like prayer, fasting, and alms.
rows.anchor: إن ( الخمر ) حقيقة في لغة العرب في التي من ماء العنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disagreement is substantial: permitting grape wine is disbelief by consensus, while permitting other intoxicants is not, since their designation as wine is disputed and their prohibition is inferential.
rows.anchor: ولقوته ووقوع الإجماع على تسمية المتخذ من العنب خمرا دون المسكر من غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grape wine itself is forbidden independently of intoxication, so all amounts, even a drop, are forbidden and its drinker is liable to the fixed penalty.
rows.anchor: عين الأول حرام غير معلول بالسكر ولا موقوف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One who denies wine’s intrinsic prohibition and says only its intoxicating effect is forbidden is an unbeliever for rejecting scripture, which calls it impurity; the cited verse is 5:90.
rows.anchor: لجحوده الكتاب إذ سماه رجسا فيه والرجس محرم العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says wine is forbidden in itself, with a version adding that its small and large amounts are alike; intoxication rules govern other drinks.
rows.anchor: وفي الخبر حرمت الخمر لعينها وفي رواية بعينها قليلها وكثيرها سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cooking cannot erase an already established prohibition; however, a cooked drink is not subject to the fixed penalty until it intoxicates, since that penalty for a small amount applies specifically to raw wine.
rows.anchor: إن الطبخ لا يؤثر لأنه للمنع من ثبوت الحرمة لا لرفعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bādhq and munṣaf, grape must cooked until less than two-thirds evaporates, are forbidden if fermented and foaming; al-Alusi says their thinness, intoxication, and pleasure attract sinners, so they are banned to prevent corruption.
rows.anchor: يسمى الباذق والمنصف وهو ما ذهب نصفه بالطبخ فحرام عندنا

rows.speaker: الأوزاعي وأكثر المعتزلة
rows.claim: Al-Awzāʿī and most Muʿtazilites permit this drink because it is pleasant and not wine; the author responds that it is intoxicating and attracts sinners, so it should be prohibited to prevent corruption.
rows.anchor: أكثر المعتزلة : إنه مباح لأنه مشروب طيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raw date infusion, called sakar, is forbidden; the author invokes the Companions’ consensus and the verse’s initial, pre-prohibition setting.
rows.anchor: نقيع التمر وهو السكروهو النيء

rows.speaker: شريك
rows.claim: Sharik argues date infusion must be permitted because the verse mentions it as a favor, which could not be forbidden; the author rejects this using consensus and the verse’s earlier setting.
rows.anchor: إنه مباح للإمتنان ولا يكون بالمحرم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reading takes the verse about date produce as a rebuke: people make intoxicating drink from it and leave wholesome provision.
rows.anchor: أتتخذون منه سكرا وتدعون رزقا حسنا

rows.speaker: الأوزاعي
rows.claim: Raw raisin infusion is forbidden once it ferments and boils, though al-Awzāʿī disputes the ruling.
rows.anchor: حرام إذا أشتد وغلى وفيه خلاف الأوزاعي

rows.speaker: أبي حنيفة وأبي يوسف
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf permit lightly cooked date or raisin nabīdh, even when fermented, if the amount is thought not to intoxicate and is drunk without revelry.
rows.anchor: عند أبي حنيفة وأبي يوسف وعند محمد والشافعي حرام

rows.speaker: محمد والشافعي
rows.claim: Muḥammad and al-Shāfiʿī forbid lightly cooked date or raisin nabīdh even in the restricted quantity described by Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf.
rows.anchor: وعند محمد والشافعي حرام

rows.speaker: الإمام الأول والثاني
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf permit drinks made from honey, figs, grains, or grape juice cooked down by two-thirds; Muḥammad and al-Shāfiʿī forbid them.
rows.anchor: حلال عند الإمام الأول والثاني وعند محمد والشافعي حرام أيضا

rows.speaker: المتأخرون
rows.claim: Later Hanafi jurists issued fatwas following Muḥammad’s prohibition for the other beverages; Ibn Wahbān says this ruling is also transmitted from all the imams.
rows.anchor: وأفتى المتأخرون بقول محمد في سائر الأشربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi’s preferred rule is that any non-grape drink is forbidden if it can intoxicate an unaccustomed drinker; a small amount is like a large one, and drinking incurs the penalty, divorce effect, and severe impurity.
rows.anchor: وعندي أن الحق الذي لا ينبغي العدول عنه

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the Ṣaḥīḥayn the Prophet answers a question about honey nabīdh that every intoxicating drink is forbidden; Abū Dāwūd reports his prohibition of every intoxicant and stupefier.
rows.anchor: كل شراب أسكر فهو حرام

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Prophetic reports say that whatever intoxicates in a large quantity is forbidden in a small quantity, and that even a palmful is forbidden if a full measure intoxicates; the author calls the reports mutually reinforcing.
rows.anchor: ما أسكر كثيره فقليله حرام وفي حديث آخر ما أسكر الفرق منه فملء الكف منه حرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi laments that contemporary drinkers favor intoxicants other than grape wine, inventing names such as amberiyya and iksīr to imagine the new names make them lawful.
rows.anchor: وقد وضعوا لها أسماء كالعنبرية والإكسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These other drinks carry a lesser prohibition than grape wine, so permitting them is not disbelief because the ruling is ijtihād-based; declaring all permitters unbelievers would leave almost nobody.
rows.anchor: نعم حرمة هذه الأشربة دون حرمة الخمر حتى لا يكفر مستحلها كما قدمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysir is a verbal noun on the pattern of mawʿid or marjiʿ, used for gambling; its derivation may refer to taking wealth easily, losing wealth, dividing shares, or a stake becoming due.
rows.anchor: مصدر ميمي منيسركالموعد والمرجع يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysir derives from taking money easily, losing wealth, dividing shares, or a stake becoming due; the gambler was called yasir because he won a share of the slaughtered camel.
rows.anchor: يسرته إذا قمرته واشتقاقه إما مناليسر

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī derives maysir from something becoming due, calling the gambler the one who owes the stake.
rows.anchor: من يسر الشيء إذا وجب والياسر الواجب بسبب القدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The traditional game used ten arrows, three blank; the other seven awarded one through seven shares of a camel divided into twenty-eight parts, while a blank-draw loser paid the entire cost.
rows.anchor: لهم عشرة أقداح هي الأزلام الفذ والتوأم

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī gives another description of the arrow names and omits al-waghd; al-Alusi relies on the account preferred by al-Zamakhsharī and many others.
rows.anchor: ونقل الأزهري كيفية أخرى لذلك ولم يذكر الوغدفي الأسماء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: An unnamed poet composed a mnemonic listing the ten gambling arrows and their shares, including the three blank arrows.
rows.anchor: كل سهام الياسرين عشره فأودعوها صحفا منشره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysir includes all gambling and wagering: backgammon, chess, children’s nuts and dice, risky lots outside division, and every kind of stake; Ibn Sīrīn says anything involving risk is maysir.
rows.anchor: كل شيء فيه خطر فهو من الميسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question concerns engaging in wine and gambling, as the answer’s “in them” makes clear; their sin comes from leading to neglected duties and committed prohibitions.
rows.anchor: المراد في تعاطيهما بلا ريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their benefits include pleasure, joy, digestion, improved complexion, sexual vigor, courage, generosity, and helping the weak; these benefits exist before and after prohibition, and no proof says prohibition removes them.
rows.anchor: من اللذة والفرح وهضم الطعام وتصفية اللون وتقوية الباه

rows.speaker: إبن أبي الدنيا
rows.claim: Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recounts a drunk man urinating into his hand and washing his face with it as if performing ablution.
rows.anchor: ذكر إبن أبي الدنيا أنه أمر بسكران وهو يبول بيده ويغسل به وجهه

rows.speaker: العباس بن مرداس
rows.claim: Al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās says in the pre-Islamic period that he would not put his ignorance into his belly by drinking, nor be a leader in the morning and a fool by evening.
rows.anchor: أنه قيل له في الجاهلية : ألا تشرب الخمر فإنها تزيد في حرارتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine distracts from remembrance and prayer, commonly produces hostility and fights, deepens into addiction, and can cause illnesses and death; loss of reason and uprightness alone suffices to make it the source of vices.
rows.anchor: ومنها صدها عن ذكر الله تعالى وعن الصلاة وإيقاعها العداوة والبغضاء غالبا

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet said to avoid wine because it is the mother of all evils; al-Alusi adds that no prophets are reliably reported to have drunk it at any time.
rows.anchor: اجتنبوا الخمر فإنها أم الخبائث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gambling takes wealth wrongfully and leads many gamblers to theft, loss of life, neglect of dependents, shameful conduct, and hidden or open enmity.
rows.anchor: أن فيه أكل الأموال بالباطل وأنه يدعو كثيرا من المقامرين إلى السرقة

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars infer that the verse itself prohibits wine because the greater harm outweighs its benefit; others add that “great sin” means punishment or its cause, which applies only to the forbidden.
rows.anchor: ذهب بعض العلماء إلى أنها هي المحرمة للخمر فإن المفسدة إذا ترجحت على المصلحة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the verse is not explicit proof of prohibition: “sin” can mean harm, and a preponderance of harm alone establishes preference, not a ban; Companions drank until the al-Māʾida prohibition.
rows.anchor: والحق أن الآية ليست نصا في التحريم كما قال قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading has “much sin” with thāʾ, and Ubayy reads “their sin is nearer than their benefit.”
rows.anchor: وقريء إثم كثير بالمثلثة وفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placing sin first, describing it as great or numerous, and delaying benefits while limiting them to people signals the dominance of the harm.
rows.anchor: وفي تقديم الإثم ووصفه بالكبر أو الكثرة وتأخير ذكر المنافع مع تخصيصها بالناس

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that companions ordered to spend in God’s path asked how much to give; before the verse, some spent everything and then lacked food or charity.
rows.anchor: أخرج إبن إسحاق عن إبن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنه أن نفرا من الصحابة أمروا بالنفقة

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل وثعلبة
rows.claim: A report through Abān from Yaḥyā says Muʿādh and Thaʿlaba, with households and dependents, asked the Prophet how much of their wealth to spend.
rows.anchor: أنه بلغه أن معاذ بن جبل وثعلبة أتيا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This question coordinates with the earlier one as a new topic; another report links it to ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ, who first asked about recipients and then about the amount to give.
rows.anchor: عطف القصة على القصة وقيل : نزلت في عمرو بن الجموح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer shows that the question asks the quality or amount of what to spend: “what” functions as a question about a description, as in asking what someone is and answering “generous.”
rows.anchor: فالمعنى يسئلونك عن صفة ما ينفقونه قل العفو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAfw is the opposite of exertion: what remains beyond need or does not burden the giver; smooth, easy-to-tread ground is also called ʿafw.
rows.anchor: وأصل العفو نقيض الجهد ولذا

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains ʿafw as the surplus remaining after providing for dependents.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية عن إبن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما الفضل من العيال

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan explains ʿafw as an amount that does not strain the giver.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن ما لا يجهد

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet says the best charity is given from sufficiency and that one should begin with those one supports; this is reported by al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Nasāʾī.
rows.anchor: خير الصدقة ما كان عن ظهر غنى وأبدأ بمن تعول

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Ibn Khuzayma’s version says the best charity leaves sufficiency, the upper hand is better, and one should begin with dependents; wife, slave, and child each plead for support.
rows.anchor: خير الصدقة ما أبقت غنى واليد العليا خير من اليد السفلى

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jābir reports that Abū Ḥuṣayn al-Sulamī offered his only egg-sized piece of mined gold as charity; after repeatedly turning him away, the Prophet took and threw it, warning against giving everything and then begging.
rows.anchor: قدم أبو حصين السلمي بمثل بيضة الحمامة من ذهب فقال

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr reads “mādhā yunfiqūn” with nominative inflection, parsing the question as subject and predicate; the others read the accusative, supplying a verb with “what” as its object to match the answer.
rows.anchor: بالرفع بتقدير المبتدأ على ( أن ماذا ينفقون ) مبتدأ وخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Thus” may point to the explanation that surplus charity is better than exhausting one’s means because it preserves resources and benefits the afterlife; it may also encompass the whole preceding discussion.
rows.anchor: المشار إليه ما يفهم من قوله سبحانه : ( قل العفو ) وإيراد صيغة البعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking “thus” to refer only to “their sin is greater than their benefit” is remote.
rows.anchor: على ما فيه لا يخفى بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf is accusative as an adjective of an omitted noun, while the definite article in “the signs” is generic: God clarifies rulings by clear revelation, another verse, or the Prophet’s explanation.
rows.anchor: والكاف في موضع النصب صفة لمحذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although a plural form might be expected to match “for you,” the demonstrative stays singular by construing it as a collective noun with singular form, for lighter expression.
rows.anchor: لكنه وحد بتأويل نحو القبيلة أو الجمع مما هو مفرد اللفظ جمع المعنى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says the singular signals every recipient of the address, as in “We pardoned you after that” (2:52); al-Alusi objects that this would create multiple addressees within one uncoordinated sentence.
rows.anchor: الإفراد للأيذان بأن المراد به كل من يتلقى الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Contemplating the signs means deriving rulings and understanding the interests and benefits attached to them; this makes reflection a fitting aim of their clarification.
rows.anchor: في الآيات فتسنتنبطوا الأحكام منها وتفهموا المصالح والمنافع المنوطة بها
